audio_caption: The audio begins with a male speaker defining open access as free, immediate, and online availability of research articles with full reuse rights, emphasizing the goal of making content accessible worldwide for reading, access, and building upon. The speaker describes the potential for people to do interesting things and work in new ways with the material, ultimately making research literature much more valuable.

The clip features one male speaker with a conversational and informative tone as he discusses the history of a model related to publishing scientific manuscripts. He mentions the expense involved and the process of distributing articles through journals, including review processes, revisions, and handling typesetting, printing, and distribution. He emphasizes the success of this method for scientific progress.

The clip starts with a male speaker discussing changes, mentioning "digitization" and how journals have "started ratcheting up the price" of subscriptions. He describes the current situation as "the theater of the absurd" regarding the amount journals want libraries to pay for subscriptions. The speaker's tone is informative and slightly critical.

The clip starts with two male speakers discussing academic journal prices, noting that they have outpaced inflation and listing expensive journal subscription costs in fields such as chemistry, physics, agriculture, geology, and botany. They point out that even some obscure journals can be very expensive. One of the speakers expresses frustration that journals are costly even though they don't produce the material, employ the writers or reviewers, questioning what the purpose of science has become. The scene concludes on the first man's final point about science spreading knowledge.

The audio begins with a man discussing the "irrational" practice of taxpayer-funded scientific research being made inaccessible to the public. He criticizes the system. A male speaker then introduces the problem of accessing research. He recalls how he, as a student, accepted this situation as the norm, but later realized there was a system preventing access. He explains that student education and the ability of professors to teach are limited by the literature they can access. He adds that less wealthy countries struggle significantly, hindering researchers and their global contributions. A different man continues to explain this situation, describing it as "research."

The audio clip features a male speaker recounting an experience where he was not convinced of the importance of public library science. He describes a family medical emergency where he was trying to find information about a particular medical treatment. Frustrated, he recounts his inability to access the necessary papers despite his scientific training. His tone transitions from explanatory to indignant as he emphasizes the moment he realized the gravity of the situation. The speaker then shifts to discussing the problem of knowing which articles are relevant before paying for them. He maintains a critical and explanatory tone. He mentions purchasing dozens of articles in the hospital room, highlighting the lack of a return policy.

The audio clip begins with a single male speaker expressing concern about a costly endeavor, questioning whether "$1200" is worth finding out if something is relevant. He suggests that doing this regularly would lead to "a big hole." The speaker then clarifies he is "not a communist," advocating for free everything and denouncing corporations. He concludes that nobody is saying "publishing is free." The speaker's tone throughout is conversational but somewhat critical.

The clip begins with a male speaker making a point about working on models, suggesting that the government already funds research and subscriptions, and that taxpayers and the government are paying for this. The speaker poses the question of why knowledge cannot be distributed broadly as opposed to restricted. The speaker is speaking in an assertive tone.

The clip begins with a male speaker describing open access, noting it's about articles being freely available to read and having "full reuse rights." He explains researchers can "build an entire new tier of tools" on the literature. He continues describing how new tools can interact with these articles, such as mining them, finding relationships, and uncovering genetic code snippets, noting that researchers wouldn't be able to do this on their own. He speaks in a tone of explanation. A second male speaker then explains that if someone wanted to do this without open access, "you couldn't" because you'd have to negotiate rights with every publisher. He speaks with a more neutral tone.

The audio clip features a male speaker discussing "an open access world" where "all this information would be open on the internet for free," and people would have "unrestricted rights" to do data mining. His tone is informative and perhaps slightly excited. No other sounds are present in the clip.

The audio clip begins with a male speaker identifying a main impediment as "the incredibly slow movement of scientific cultural practices," noting that scientists can be "very conservative in terms of changing their practices." He continues to elaborate on how the community voices support for openness while still valuing nature papers and journals with high impact factors, which, in his view, allows some journals to resist community pressure. The male speaker shifts to the current scientific publishing model, noting there's "no evidence that it is optimal," and advocates experimenting with various scientific publishing systems. He adds that corporations may come up with solutions before governments do, open to creative solutions from any source. His tone is analytical and thoughtful. The audio transitions to another male speaker, who advocates that graduate students start conversations with their research teams and PIs about the importance of making their research accessible, highlighting the benefit of increased visibility and potential for others to build on their work, emphasizing that it benefits both the reader and the researcher. This speaker has a slightly more upbeat and persuasive tone. The audio ends with a man simply saying "I."

The clip begins with a man speaking in an assured tone, asserting his belief that "scientific knowledge spreads and increases best if there are no restrictions on access" and emphasizing his desire for the "discovery of new scientific knowledge to happen faster," stating that "openness helps accelerate that." Subsequently, another male speaker enters, adopting a more conversational tone. He discusses publishing in subscription journals, but points out that "even if you don't publish in an open access journal, that you can still make, you know, the text of the article itself freely available, so that people can at least read it and get access to it." The clip concludes with indistinct music.
